title: Japanese police crash data link AEB on six best-selling car models to 20% lower odds of fatal or serious pedestrian injury
summary: In Japanese police data for 2016 to 2019, AEB on six best-selling car models was linked to 20% lower odds of fatal or serious injury for struck pedestrians; cyclists showed no clear change.
account: H. Inada of the University of Tokyo and M. Ichikawa of the University of Tsukuba used national police-reported data from Japan for 2016 to 2019 on crashes between cars and pedestrians or cyclists. They focused on six best-selling car models that offered automatic emergency braking (AEB) as an option, and they compared injury severity in crashes with and without AEB on the striking car, adjusting for confounders. Among 4,131 pedestrians, AEB was associated with 20% lower odds of a fatal or serious injury (adjusted odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.996). Among 6,659 cyclists, the authors found no significant association (adjusted odds ratio 0.91). Accident Analysis & Prevention published the study online on 10 May 2025. The study is cross-sectional and covers only crashes that happened, so it measures injury severity and cannot count crashes that AEB avoided. The upper bound of the pedestrian estimate is close to no effect, and the authors call for studies of newer systems that detect cyclists.
purpose: AEB is built to brake automatically to avoid or soften a collision. The milder pedestrian injuries that the study measured were within that purpose.
